messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping standardized coefficients
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping standardized coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Isaac

Here is an example code for something like that. Note that is you have a CFA and use std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, the covariance = correlation

####
library(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

myFun <- function(x){
  ## get all parameter estimates, including standardized
  pts <- parameterestimates(x, standardized = T)
  return(pts[22:24,"std.all"]) ## select the rows for the correlations, the standardized
}

l.boot <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R=100, type="bollen.stine",
                          FUN=myFun)
l.boot ## is a 3 column matrix, each row is a bootstrap, and each row is a different correlation

## you can estimate the mean, sd, and quantiles with something like this
apply(l.boot, 2, FUN=function(x)c(mean=mean(x),sd=sd(x),quantile(x,probs=c(.025,.5,.975))))

bye

> Is it allow to free an intercept for only one group in the second occasion? 2) If yes, how do code this?
> With regard to post I mentioned above, I would free the intercepts for every group in the second occasion.

You already figured out the syntax, but yes, you can free in just one group at the second occasion if that is what the data suggest.  You can think of this like a MANCOVA.  I don't know the order of your groups, but the interpretation of one freed intercept at Time 2 would be something like the following:

> Given (controlling for) the common factor, there is an effect of complex language when using star ratings on variable 4.

That is, freeing an intercept in 1 of 4 experimental groups implies an interaction between wording and response format.

messages.subject: Re: Too many variables
messages.subject_clean: Too many variables
messages.body_plain:
Samantha,
There is a lot going on here.

First, "too complicated" is too coarse a description.  It is important to distinguish different kinds of being too complicated, as I have tried to do in previous posts.

A better way to think about sample size is in relation to the number of parameters that you are trying to estimate.  I am not sure how many observed variables you are modeling, it looks like more than 41.  You can count your parameters as shown below.  There is no fixed rule-of-thumb but introductory SEM books can provide some rough guidelines (e.g., 1:10, 1:20).  You can compute the number of variances and covariances as (k * (k + 1))/2 where k is the number of observed variables.

lavInstpect(my.lavaan.fit.object, what='free')

All of your fit statistics and indices are sending a consistent message:  You model does not fit.  If the model is misspecified, you probably need to address that before you can make sense of anything else.  Build up the model step-by-step as described in my first post and watch for when the poor fit starts to show up.

Once you include covariates and outcomes, you are out of CFA territory and need to give up the idea of correlations.  Your factors are now endogenous variables that depend upon the covariates and the outcomes depend upon the factors (I am guessing the second order factors?).

I do not think that it is a good idea to model the covariates and outcomes in separate models.  Regression assumes that any omitted variables are exactly uncorrelated with the predictors in the model, in the population.  That may not be plausible.

If your sample size is too small -- and it may be, I am not sure, intuitively it feels to me like more of an N=1000 model than an N = 500 model and you are below 500 -- then you might consider the following alternative.  Sum the items to form scale scores in place of the first order factors.  Model these using the current second order factors and first order factors.  This will reduce the number of parameters that you are estimating.

One way to evaluate this is to simulate data from your model and then fit the model to the simulated data.  This will help you understand how the model behaves when the hypothesis is correct.  See the simulateData() function.  The standard errors for the parameters, both using your data and simulated data, may offer the best guide.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Elias,
If you have sufficient confidence in your model that ill fit leads you to first question the data, then it may be that there is nothing to be gained from fitting the model to the data.  The usual situation is the opposite: We are more confident in the data than the model and use the data to test the model.  Resolving ill fit is not a simple mechanical process like replacing the batteries in a flash light.  It is instead a complex highly-context-specific task of scientific inference that takes experience, skill, and practice.  If you have not done so already, I would highly recommend consulting a detailed introduction to this process such as can be found in Rex Kline's text "Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling".  Be sure to obtain the 4th edition.  A general strategy might be to build up the model piece by piece in an attempt to localize the sources of ill fit.  However, if you think that you might be reading the data incorrectly, first compare the sample statistics from the lavaan fit object to the corresponding statistics obtained outside of lavaan by using lavInspect() to extract the statistics from the fit object.

Keith

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

> I'm confused by your use of "on the other hand," which suggests you might be testing constraints in the wrong order.  First, compare ModUn and ModHomog.  Because that test is not significant, you can't reject the null hypothesis that the effects of covariates on the latent slope do not differ across groups.  In other words, the effect of a covariate on the slope (i.e., the 2-way interaction between Time and the covariate) does not depend on Group (i.e., there is no evidence of a 3-way interaction between Group, Time, and a covariate).

My apologies for the confusion. The steps I took were as follows:
I compared the unrestricted model (ModUn) to a model with restricted predictor effects on the latent slope (ModHomog)
(restricted like this: s~ c(a1,a1)*X1+c(b1,b1)*X2...)
These models did not differ significantly, therefore I proceeded to test whether the ModHomog differed from the model that in addition restricts the latent slope
(additional restriction like this: s~ c(x1,x1)*1)
These models did not differ significantly.
Therefore I concluded no significant differences between groups are present, with regard to the effects of the covariates on the latent slope.

> If you also want to test whether the mean of the latent intercept differs across groups (i.e., whether there is a significant "main" effect of Group on the outcome at Time 0), you first need to establish whether the effect of covariate(s) on the latent intercepts differs across groups (i.e., whether there is a covariate by Group 2-way interaction).  To do so, you can continue to use the model in which the latent slope's mean was constrained across groups (since you failed to reject that null hypothesis) as the baseline model (i.e., the new "unconstrained model" for the next test).  Compare that model to a model in which the effect of each covariate on the latent intercept is equal across groups (just like you did for effects on the latent slope).  If that constraint holds, you can then additionally constrain the mean of the latent intercept to equality across groups to see if fit gets worse (which would indicate a significant main effect of Group).

We are not interested in intercept differences, since these intercepts represent scores before intervention (and before randomization). I misinterpreted the constraint of intercept in the post before.

About the complete model:
Additionally I wish to add time-variant predictors to the model, as follows:

model3<- '

i =~ 1*T0_FCRI_S + 1*T1_FCRI_S + 1*T2_FCRI_S
s =~ 0*T0_FCRI_S + 1*T1_FCRI_S + 2*T2_FCRI_S

#regressions
i ~ Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ etc.
s ~ Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ etc.

#time-varying covariates
T0_FCRI_S ~ T0_PDQ_PH + T0_PDQ_AT + etc.
T1_FCRI_S ~ T1_PDQ_PH + T1_PDQ_AT + etc.
T2_FCRI_S ~ T2_PDQ_PH + T2_PDQ_AT + etc.
'

I intend to proceed with this model by going through the same steps as mentioned above (starting with the omnibus test).

For future research, would you propose to test the maximal model immediately (including all (time-variant and time-invariant) predictors) or build up from smaller models (which I now did)?
Testing the full model first might give a more complete representation.
I am interested what your thoughts are on this.

Yours sincerely,

Rosalie van Woezik

messages.body_plain:
Well, you can't generate data with ones on the diagonal of the beta matrix so that would need to be fixed regardless. Looking at your code, the other issue is probably the specification of RTS and RPS in the model command. These specifying the correlation matrices of the latent variables and the observed variables, which simsem attempt to translate into covariance matrices. For simple models this works well, for a more complex model this occasionally has issues (specifically combinations of the beta and lambda matrix might imply negative population variances). I think that's what's happening here. If you change the sim command to use the given psi and theta matrices as covariance matrices (see below) things work fine.

CFA.Model <- simsem::model(LY=LY, BE=BE, PS=RPS, TE=RTE, AL= AL ,modelType="SEM")

messages.subject: Re: lavaan error cfa
messages.subject_clean: lavaan error cfa
messages.body_plain:
Your model appears to suffer from empirical underidentification--the method cannot obtain unique estimates for model parameters because, even though the model structure would be identified, in your data set it is not. A rule of thumb for statistical identification of a factor model is that each factor has 2 congeneric (no cross-loadings, no correlated uniquenesses) indicators AND strong enough loadings AND each factor is correlated with at least 1 other variable. So your model, with just 2 indicators per factor, is right on the edge of failing identification. Even 1 small loading or 1 factor with no strong correlations with the other factors will cause identification to fail. Of course, the estimates you are seeing are not final estimates, but the evidence in those estimates--including pairs of indicators where 1 loading is super-big and 1 loading is tiny, and the apparently very small factor covariances--all suggests that this is your problem.
This could be a matter of poor starting values--though lavaan's default starting values generally work well. So you might try adding starting values to your syntax. I suggest that you set starting values for loadings at , say, the square root of half each indicator's variance, set starting values for uniquenesses (residual variance) at half of each indicator's loading, and set starting values for factor covariances at about 0.5 (since you are standardizing factors). Make sure that positive correlations for factors make sense given your data--you don't want the estimation process to take any factor covariances through the zero point.
It may just be that the factor model is not a good choice for these data. Fit indices tell you something about teh suitability of the model for the data, but these performance issues tell you something else.

messages.body_plain:
> For future research, would you propose to test the maximal model immediately (including all (time-variant and time-invariant) predictors) or build up from smaller models (which I now did)?
> Testing the full model first might give a more complete representation.
> I am interested what your thoughts are on this.

SEMNET would be a good place to post this general SEM question

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

But I agree with your intuition.  In OLS or multilevel regression framework, one can add predictors sequentially to test effects of one set after controlling for another.  But in SEM, you cannot compare the fit of models to different (subsets of) data, so you are probably better off entering the entire set of covariates at once to test their effects.  But it is perfectly reasonable to first build your LGCM without any covariates, to assess assumptions of linearity, variability in random effects, etc.  Then add the covariates to see what predicts the random effects (i.e., latent intercept and slope) -- but recall you cannot compare the fit of that model to the fit of a model that does not include covariates at all.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping standardized coefficients
messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping standardized coefficients
messages.body_plain:
> 1) When bootstrapping for the correlation coefficient many of the bootstrapped samples seem to be unreasonable (i.e. <-1 or >1). How would you suggest to deal with that (if my end goal is to obtain a CI for the correlation)?

Sampling error can lead to values near the border to cross the border.  Is the correlation out of bounds in the original sample?  The bootstrap CI should reflect the true bootstrap sampling distribution, so include all samples.  As long as the CI includes plausible values (correlations with +/- 1), then you cannot reject the null hypothesis that the true population value is a correlation with a reasonable value.

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

> 2) How many bootstrapped samples would you say are necessary? Will this matter as a result of which bootstrapping technique am I using?

Since you are using the bootstrap distribution to estimate tail quantities (which are unlikely by definition), you need a lot.  If you are calculating a 95% CI, then you are estimating it from the bottom and top 2.5% of the data.  If you have 1000 bootstrap samples, then your estimate of each confidence limit is based on 25 bootstrap samples.  Would you be comfortable estimating a population mean with only N = 25 people, especially when it costs you nothing but computation time to "gather" a larger sample?  I have seen some (e.g., Preach and Hayes) advise 5000 bootstrap samples, which bases the confidence limits on 125 in each tail.  I would be more comfortable that sampling error in that quantity is sufficiently small, regardless of whether the percentile or bias-corrected boostrap CI is calculated.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Robust CFI Discrepancy
messages.subject_clean: Robust CFI Discrepancy
messages.body_plain:
Good morning,

I'm running a full SEM correcting for non-normality with Satorra-Bentler. In trying to confirm some of the robust statistics, I keep running into an issue in that the robust CFI I'm calculating using information in the lavaan "test" slot differs from the value reported by the print.fit.measures() function as seen here: https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_fit_measures.R.

>From the lav_fit_measures() function shown at the link above, the robust CFI is calculated (see code line 373) using using Equation (15) here <https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Patricia_Brosseau-Liard/publication/266237769_Adjusting_Incremental_Fit_Indices_for_Nonnormality/links/580fafc808aee15d4912109b.pdf>.

The subroutine for calculating the robust CFI is given as:

if("cfi.robust" %in% fit.measures) {
if(TEST[[2]]$test %in% c("satorra.bentler", "yuan.bentler")) {

                    # see Brosseau-Liard & Savalei MBR 2014, equation 15

                    # what to do if X2 = 0 and df = 0? in this case,
                   # the scaling factor (ch) will be NA, and we get NA
                   # (instead of 1)
                   if(X2 < .Machine$double.eps && df == 0) {
                       ch <- 0
                   } else {
                       ch <- TEST[[2]]$scaling.factor
                   }
                   cb <- fit.indep@test[[2]]$scaling.factor

                    t1 <- max( c(X2 - (ch*df), 0) )
                   t2 <- max( c(X2 - (ch*df), X2.null - (cb*df.null), 0) )
                   if(is.na(t1) || is.na(t2)) {
                       indices["cfi.robust"] <- NA
                   } else if(t1 == 0 && t2 == 0) {
                       indices["cfi.robust"] <- 1
                   } else {
                       indices["cfi.robust"] <- 1 - t1/t2
                   }
               } else {
                   indices["cfi.robust"] <- NA
               }
           }

I'm looking specifically at t1 and t2 values. The equation given in Brosseau-Liard & Savalei MBR 2014, equation 15 is

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-FdN0bqOMf94/WgGlK3LA4SI/AAAAAAAADAM/tl8RfWSeJcsCBSDFd2PQmf9R271bey5cACLcBGAs/s1600/Screen%2BShot%2B2017-11-07%2Bat%2B7.20.26%2BAM.png>
I'm reading this as T_ML,H is the Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square or T statistic for the hypothesized model and the T_ML,B is the same quantity for the baseline / null model. the c quantities are the respective correction factors for the theoretical and baseline / null models, respectively and df is likewise degrees of freedom.

If my fitted hypothesis model object were named epm.sem.fit.d.mlm, I'm drawing the said quantities from the epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]] slot of the fitted object with the T value coming from the epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]]$stat, degrees of freedom from epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]]$df, and Satorra-Bentler scaling factor from epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]]$scaling.factor. In other words,

chisq.fit = epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]]$stat
df.fit = epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]]$df
sf.fit = epm.sem.fit.d.mlm@test[[2]]$scaling.factor

If the fitted null (independence model) object were named epm.ov.null.fit, I'm drawing the relevant quantities from epm.ov.null.fit@test[[2]]$stat, epm.ov.null.fit@test[[2]]$df, and epm.ov.null.fit@test[[2]]$scaling.factor. In other words,

chisq.null = epm.ov.null.fit@test[[2]]$stat
df.null = epm.ov.null.fit@test[[2]]$df
sf.null = epm.ov.null.fit@test[[2]]$scaling.factor

If the numerator and denominator of the equation above were named cfi.num and cfi.denom, respectively, I would calculate these quantities as

cfi.num = (chisq.fit - df.fit * sf.fit)
cfi.denom = (chisq.null - df.null * sf.null)

The robust CFI (cfi.rob) value would then be

cfi.rob = 1 - (cfi.num / cfi.denom)

It looks like the function calculating this value looks for the maximum between the cfi.num and cfi.denom and chooses that as the actual denominator to avoid producing values beyond 1, which makes perfect sense. The actual values associated with each of the quantities above when drawing from the fitted object are:

chisq.fit
[1] 1826.315

> df.fit
[1] 1105

> sf.fit
[1] 1.258276

> chisq.null
[1] 5791.451

> df.null
[1] 1176

> sf.null
[1] 1.390944

> cfi.num
[1] 435.9202

> cfi.denom
[1] 4155.701

Plugging this information into the above then results in a robust cfi value of

cfi.rob
[1] 0.8951031

or approximately .90 when rounded. When calling the summary() function and passing in the fitted lavaan object, which I believe calls the print.fit.measures() function noted above, the snippet of results relevant to the issue returned is

summary(epm.sem.fit.d.mlm, fit.measures = TRUE)
lavaan (0.5-23.1097) converged normally after 101 iterations

                                                  Used       Total
  Number of observations                           231         254

  Estimator                                         ML      Robust
  Minimum Function Test Statistic             2298.008    1826.315
  Degrees of freedom                              1105        1105
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000       0.000

  Robust Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI)                            0.850

The Robust CFI values reported by the summary call passing in the lavaan fit object prints a robust value of .859, which seems to have transposed the second and third decimal. I should note that the print null chi square is slightly different than the value extracted from running the null model myself, but the differences are minor. Using the printed result instead of the extracted result still produces a robust CFI value of .895. I've also tried calling fitMeasures() directly instead of the summary() function and the results returned match the results presented by the summary() function:

messages.body_plain:
Your n is 5,000, so your power to detect discrepancies is fairly high.
Degrees of freedom come from constraints. The three constraints in your model are the non-paths from
V051, V052 and V053 to V001. Your current model says that the partial correlations of these three predictors
with V001 are 0, after accounting for their covariance with V008, which does predict V001. You could use
the modIndices function to get estimates of exactly how each constraint is affecting your chi-square. Or you
could estimate the model including those 3 paths and then make a judgment whether they have practical
significance.

Hi lavaan community,

I am wondering if there is an update on whether lavaan can fit negative binomial instead of regular regression. My outcome measure is highly (positively) skewed. Since FIML cannot be used for binary options (if dichotomized), I am trying to figure out if I can use highly skewed outcome measures as they are.

Here is my model:

p16a18c24 <- '
# direct effect
myOutcome ~ c*myPredictor
# mediator
myMediator1 ~ a1*myPredictor
myOutcome ~ b1*myMediator1
myMediator2 ~ a2*myPredictor
myOutcome ~ b2*myMediator2
myMediator3 ~ a3*myPredictor
myOutcome ~ b3*myMediator3
# variances: any variable that was listed as DV
myOutcome ~~ myOutcome
myMediator1 ~~ myMediator1
myMediator2 ~~ myMediator2
myMediator3 ~~ myMediator3
# covariances: mediators who are (positively) correlated with each other
myMediator1 ~~ myMediator2
myMediator2 ~~ myMediator3
myMediator3 ~~ myMediator1
# intercepts: *1, only for DVs
myOutcome ~ 1
myMediator1 ~ 1
myMediator2 ~ 1
myMediator3 ~ 1
# indirect effects (a*b)
ab1 := a1*b1
ab2 := a2*b2

# total effect

> I am wondering if there is an update on whether lavaan can fit negative binomial instead of regular regression.

No, and that is unlikely to change anytime in the near future (i.e., next few years).  The Bayesian option I alluded to in September handles missing data quite nicely, because JAGS automatically treats missing values as additional parameters to be estimated, with priors equivalent to the likelihoods specified for the corresponding observed data.  OpenMx also is quite flexible, so you could program it yourself, if you are capable:

http://openmx.ssri.psu.edu/thread/1433

messages.subject: Re: Reliability, ordinal omega?
messages.subject_clean: Reliability, ordinal omega?
messages.body_plain:
> would be ordinal estimates?

Not sure if you have the latest development version of semTools installed, but this is from the latest ?reliability help page:

> Regarding categorical indicators, coefficient alpha and AVE are calculated based on polychoric correlations. The coefficient alpha from this function may be not the same as the standard alpha calculation for categorical items. Researchers may check the alpha function in the psych package for the standard coefficient alpha calculation.  Item thresholds are not accounted for. Coefficient omega for categorical items, however, is calculated by accounting for both item covariances and item thresholds using Green and Yang's (2009, formula 21) approach. Three types of coefficient omega indicate different methods to calculate item total variances. The original formula from Green and Yang is equivalent to ω_3 in this function. Green and Yang did not propose a method for calculating reliability with a mixture of categorical and continuous indicators, and we are currently unaware of an appropriate method. Therefore, when reliability detects both categorical and continuous indicators in the model, an error is returned. If the categorical indicators load on a different factor(s) than continuous indicators, then reliability can be calculated separately for those scales by fitting separate models and submitting each to the reliability function.

So only that version of omega takes thresholds into account, giving an estimate of the reliability of the sum of those categorical items.

> I saw ordinal alpha and ordinal omega calculated in the package
> userfriendlyscience
>
> with the function
> scaleReliability

As that help page shows, it is just a wrapper around the MBESS package's ci.reliability() function, which is written by the same author (and uses the same source code) of the reliability() function in semTools.  So the same applies.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

The coefficient alpha from this function may be not the same as the standard alpha calculation for categorical items. Researchers may check the alpha function in the psych package for the standard coefficient alpha calculation.  Item thresholds are not accounted for. Coefficient omega for categorical items, however, is calculated by accounting for both item covariances and item thresholds using Green and Yang's (2009, formula 21) approach. Three types of coefficient omega indicate different methods to calculate item total variances. The original formula from Green and Yang is equivalent to ω_3 in this function. Green and Yang did not propose a method for calculating reliability with a mixture of categorical and continuous indicators, and we are currently unaware of an appropriate method. Therefore, when reliability detects both categorical and continuous indicators in the model, an error is returned. If the categorical indicators load on a different factor(s) than continuous indicators, then reliability can be calculated separately for those scales by fitting separate models and submitting each to the reliability function.

messages.subject: Re: sim () function produces warning about negative ov variances
messages.subject_clean: sim () function produces warning about negative ov variances
messages.body_plain:
> Do you have any ideas what might be wrong about my models?

Probably nothing.  You have specified some residual variances that are very close to zero (e.g., auf.ind2 ~~ 0.050*auf.ind2), and you have some very small sample sizes (as low as N = 50).  So estimates of near-zero variances are quite likely to be negative in several samples just due to sampling error.  Try looking at the M and SD of the sampling distribution of that estimate across replications -- you can probably guess that sometimes it is going negative.

Because you know the cause is just sampling error, you don't need to worry about it.  If it were a single real data set, you would want to test whether the negative variance is consistent with sampling error (if not, then model misspecification is the other alternative explanation).

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Convergence problem only with robust estimators
messages.subject_clean: Convergence problem only with robust estimators
messages.body_plain:
My initial guess was right:

The model where you use se="robust.sem" uses listwise deletion, and
fails to converge.

The model where you use estimator = "MLF" also uses listwise deletion,
and fails to converge.

If you use all the data, using fiml, the model does converge. For the
'robust' version, you need to use se="robust.huber.white", together with
missing="ml". (You can also use estimator="MLR" which will imply
se="robust.huber.white")

For estimator = "MLF", you also need to add the missing="ml" flag (if
you want fiml). Note that the informatin="expected" argument will be
(silently) ignored here, as you are use first.order information instead.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
I think the problem is just that you are putting constraints in syntax that would only apply to the configural model, which then get in the way when that same model is adapted for metric, scalar, and strict models.  Did you know there are arguments to cfa() that set the latent scale by fixing factor variances instead of factor loadings?  See the ?lavOptions help page for lots of useful defaults to turn on/off.  This works fine for fitting the model you want to fit:

myUWES9 <- '
vig =~ UWES9.UWES1. + UWES9.UWES2. + UWES9.UWES5.
ded =~ UWES9.UWES3. + UWES9.UWES4. + UWES9.UWES7.abs =~ UWES9.UWES6. + UWES9.UWES8. + UWES9.UWES9
'
myOrds <- c("UWES9.UWES1.","UWES9.UWES2.","UWES9.UWES5.",

            "UWES9.UWES3.","UWES9.UWES4.","UWES9.UWES7.",
            "UWES9.UWES6.","UWES9.UWES8.","UWES9.UWES9.")

measurementInvarianceCat(UWES9, data = df.UWES9, estimator = "WLSMV",

                         group = "Country", std.lv = TRUE, ordered = myOrds)

The problem with your 2nd-order factor model is that it contains a 2nd-order factor.  This function is not set up to handle that, so you will have to write the syntax yourself.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Bootstrapping standardized coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the detailed answers. I'll explain my model in more detail:

It's a simple structural model where instead of a full measurement model, I have a good estimate of the reliability which I use to specify the residual variances. So let's say I have an observed variables O1 and O2 for N participants, and I want to estimate the true correlation between T1 and T2, as well as the predicted values of T1 and T2 for each participant. I know the reliabilities of both variables, so I can specify:
in r:

E1=(1-rel1)*var(O1)
E2=(1-rel2)*var(O2)

and in lavaan (by using paste to insert E1 and E2):

T1=~1*O1
T2=~1*O2
O1~~E1*O1
O2~~E2*O2

So my question is what would be the best way to get CIs for the correlation rT1T2, and for the individuals' estimates of T1i and T2i?
I'm not sure how the bootstrap function works in lavaan exactly, but I understand now that it might use incorrect estimates of E1 and E2 unless these values are also bootstrapped in some way. I was able to work out a simple bootstrap myself - by sampling with replacement from the dataset, calculating E1 and E2, and running the sem model for R times. This may work for the correlation, but surely this won't work well for getting predicted estimates for individual participants (lavPredict), because in simple bootstrap I get different participants each time...

If anyone has any idea what would be the best way to deal with this issue - I'll be very thankful.

Isaac.

On Monday, November 6, 2017 at 2:45:08 PM UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > 1) When bootstrapping for the correlation coefficient many of the bootstrapped samples seem to be unreasonable (i.e. <-1 or >1). How would you suggest to deal with that (if my end goal is to obtain a CI for the correlation)?
>
> Sampling error can lead to values near the border to cross the border.  Is the correlation out of bounds in the original sample?  The bootstrap CI should reflect the true bootstrap sampling distribution, so include all samples.  As long as the CI includes plausible values (correlations with +/- 1), then you cannot reject the null hypothesis that the true population value is a correlation with a reasonable value.
>
> http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0049124112442138
>
> > 2) How many bootstrapped samples would you say are necessary? Will this matter as a result of which bootstrapping technique am I using?
>
> Since you are using the bootstrap distribution to estimate tail quantities (which are unlikely by definition), you need a lot.  If you are calculating a 95% CI, then you are estimating it from the bottom and top 2.5% of the data.  If you have 1000 bootstrap samples, then your estimate of each confidence limit is based on 25 bootstrap samples.  Would you be comfortable estimating a population mean with only N = 25 people, especially when it costs you nothing but computation time to "gather" a larger sample?  I have seen some (e.g., Preach and Hayes) advise 5000 bootstrap samples, which bases the confidence limits on 125 in each tail.  I would be more comfortable that sampling error in that quantity is sufficiently small, regardless of whether the percentile or bias-corrected boostrap CI is calculated.
>

messages.body_plain:
> For the second-order latent model, can I use the proposed steps in this <http://pareonline.net/getvn.asp?v=19&n=7> article?

I wouldn't because it relies on the group.equal shortcut that only works in simple cases.

I would just focus on testing measurement invariance in the first-order model like you were.  Once you establish (at least partial) invariance in the first order factors, then specify a 2nd-order factor model with the first-order measurement constraints already in place.  Consider that the configural model for the 2nd-order factor, then add constraints on those loadings and intercepts one step at a time to test the decrement in fit.  You can add constraints in the model syntax using a vector of identical labels (one per group).  From the lavaan tutorial:

> Constraining a single parameter to be equal across groups
>
> If you want to constrain one or more parameters to be equal across groups, you need to give them the same label. For example, to constrain the factor loading of the indicator x3 to be equal across (two) groups, you can write:
> HS.model <- '
>   visual =~ x1 + x2 + c(v3,v3)*x3
>   textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>   speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
>
> Again, identical labels imply identical parameters, both within and across groups.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: LISREL MIMIC model with no disturbance term
messages.subject_clean: LISREL MIMIC model with no disturbance term
messages.body_plain:
Fornell and Bookstein (1982) were not wrong! Goldberger (1970) shows that, in the case of a MIMIC model with no disturbance term and correlated y-indicator disturbances, maximum-likelihood estimation is identical to modified generalized least-squares estimation and the computations are intimately related to those of canonical correlation analysis (see Hauser and Goldberger, 1971, pp.104-106 and Appendix). Also Bagozzi et al. (1981) show that the first canonical variable pair can be expressed as a MIMIC model (see pp. 443-445). On the other side, in the case of two latent variables with both formative indicators (which corresponds to mode B in PLS-PM), the PLS algorithm converges to the first canonical components of canonical correlation analysis (see Tenenhaus et al., 2005, p.194). So here it is!!

References

Bagozzi R., Fornell C. and Larcker D.F. (1981) Canonical Correlation Analysis as a Special Case of a Structural Relations Model, Multivariate Behavioral Research, 16, 437-454.

Fornell C. and Bookstein F.L. (1982) Two Structural Equation Models: LISREL and PLS Applied to Consumer Exit-Voice Theory, Journal of Marketing Research, Vol. 19, No. 4, Special Issue on Causal Modeling, pp.440-452.

Goldberger, A.S. (1970) Criteria and constraints in multivariate regression. Workshop Paper EME 7026. Social Systems Research Institute, Madison: University of Wisconsin.

Hauser R.M. and Goldberger S. (1971) The Treatment of Unobservable Variables in Path Analysis, in Sociological Methodology, H.L. Costner, ed. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 81-117.

Tenenhaus M., Esposito Vinzi V., Chatelin Y.M. and Lauro C. (2005) PLS path modeling, Comput. Statist. Data Anal., 48, 159–205.

messages.subject: number of dfs in baseline model changes if including the covariance of the predictors in regression
messages.subject_clean: number of dfs in baseline model changes if including the covariance of the predictors in regression
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

this question concerns the computation of dfs in the baseline model. As you can see below, the dfs in the baseline model change if I include a covariance of predictors in the regression manually in the model. As the number of the dfs decreases in the baseline model, so does of course the CFI (in our empirical example by about .10, which is why this is relevant to us). In the lavaan tutorial (http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html), the covariances are not included.

I would like to know,

- which is the correct way to do it? Should I include the covariances of the predictors in the model specification?

- why does the number of dfs change in the baseline model? (Pointing me to some literature would also do it :)

Thank you very much,
Best,
Kai

# no covariance ------------------------------------------------------

HS_model_nocov <- '
  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
'
fit_nocov <- cfa(HS_model_nocov, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit_nocov)["baseline.df"] == (6*5)/2 # TRUE

# here, the baseline dfs are computed based on the formula (n*(n-1))/2.

# regression ---------------------------------------------------------

HS_model_regr <- '
  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  visual ~ x8 + x9
'
fit_regr <- cfa(HS_model_regr, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit_regr)["baseline.df"]

# here, the dfs are 27 instead of 28.

# regression with cov ------------------------------------------------

HS_model_regr_cov <- '
  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  visual ~ x8 + x9
  x8 ~~ x9
'

fit_regr_cov <- cfa(HS_model_regr_cov, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit_regr_cov)["baseline.df"]

# here the dfs are again 28, as we expected them to be.

# cfi ----------------------------------------------------------------

# this is only relevant for the computation of the CFI, as far as I know:

fitMeasures(fit_regr)["cfi"]
fitMeasures(fit_regr_cov)["cfi"]

messages.body_plain:
Kai--
     Covariates are meant to be exogenous variables. Their distribution is not explained by the model. Your syntax plays with the lavaan:::sem() function's defaults. The former syntax treats the variables as exogenous, while the latter treats them as endogenous variables to be explained.
     There are implications beyond CFI. ML estimation is actually conditional on the distributions of any exogenous covariates. At a minimum, treating them as exogenous means that any nonnormality in these variables is ignored, while treating them as variables to be explained means that any nonnormality would be weighed in developing ML fit. So changing the designation of these variables does change the estimation in profound ways.
     The important thing is to decide if the variables are exogenous or not. That is a conceptual / theoretical question. If these variables are, say, experimental treatments, then their behavior is in the hands of the researcher--it is not an issue for the model to explain.

messages.body_plain:
Edward,
    I do know that composite-based methods and factor-based methods are not identical and relate to two completely different philosophies. That's why I was certainly surprised to read that under special assumptions MIMIC with only one latent construct and PLS-PM with two formative latent constructs give the same results (in terms of weighs/loadings and latent scores). I wanted to prove it myself with numbers but also needed to understand the reason. The papers I quoted helped me to see the connection of both methods to canonical correlation analysis, so that now the equivalence makes sense. This doesn't mean that the two approaches are the same, but that in this specific case and particularly when you don't know the origin of the data, you can interpret the results according to one or the other method.

On 11/10/2017 05:20 PM, David Giofrè wrote:
> Hello everybody,
> I was thrilled by this new paper "Factor Score Path Analysis" by Ines
> Devlieger and Yves Rosseel (2017). I would like to perform a Factor
> Score Path Analysis using lavaan, so I was wondering whether the lavaan
> syntax is available or not.

As an experimental feature, lavaan includes the function fsr() (for
factor score regression). See

?fsr

for more information.

fsr() will normally only provide point estimates for the structural part
of the model. There are no standard errors (yet). Bootstrapping would
certainly work, but you will have to set this up yourself.

Eventually, fsr() may be used as a replacement for sem() in certain
cases, but we are not there yet.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Kai,
Thank you for asking this question.  It is not behavior that I would have anticipated either.  Ed tends to be correct about these sorts of things, but I am also interested in understanding the behavior at a less abstract level.  I have not yet located the code that specifies the baselinel model, which would answer the question.  Nor have I located a way to extract the baseline model specification after the fact.  However, I did succeed in reproducing the baseline models.

HS_model_null <- '
  x1 ~~ x1
  x2 ~~ x2
  x3 ~~ x3
  x4 ~~ x4
  x5 ~~ x5
  x6 ~~ x6
  x8 ~~ x8
  x9 ~~ x9
  # no covaraince between x8 and x9
'

fit_null <- cfa(HS_model_null, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit_null)[c("df", "chisq")]

HS_model_null_cov <- '
  x1 ~~ x1
  x2 ~~ x2
  x3 ~~ x3
  x4 ~~ x4
  x5 ~~ x5
  x6 ~~ x6
  x8 ~~ x8
  x9 ~~ x9
  x8 ~~ x9 # free covariance
'

fit_null_cov <- cfa(HS_model_null_cov, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit_null_cov)[c("df", "chisq")]

I was unable to reproduce the impact of covariances between exogenous variables with a path model.  Likewise, CFA models with and without correlated uniquenesses produce the same baseline model.  So the effect appears specific to exogenous variable covariances in latent variable models.

You can use the baseline parameter to the fitMeasures() function to obtain fit measures for a baseline model that you specify.

fitMeasures(fit_regr, baseline.model=fit_null) # baseline df = 28

Keith

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Your model is a normal mediation model and none of the regressors and endogenous with respect to their dependent variable. (The term endogenous variable can have different meanings in this context.)

If I understood your example correctly, you want to model regression of F3 on F1 and F2, using F2 as an instrument for F1. That model would not be identified and cannot be meaningfully estimated with ML and cannot be estimated at all using 2SLS. But more generally, if you want to do instrumental variable models, you need to free the correlations between the error term of the DV and the endogenous explanatory variable. This will not give you 2SLS estimates because Lavaan does not do 2SLS, but the ML estimates should be close to 2SLS estimates.

I think that you need to clarify a bit more what you want to do.

Mikko

Kai,
There is a saying in the Python community: Explicit is better than implicit.

https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0020/

Using the approach that Terrence suggested, I explored your models a little further.  To provide a more controlled environment, I switched to lavaan() with only a  minimal set of convenience parameters.  (I am not sure that it is ever a good idea to use cfa() to fit a model other than a CFA.)  If fit 3 models:
Model 1:  Omitted covariance
Model 2:  Included free covariance
Model 3: Included fixed zero covariance

HS_model_regr <- '
visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
visual ~ x8 + x9
'

HS_model_regr_cov <- '
  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  visual ~ x8 + x9
  x8 ~~ x9
'

HS_model_regr_nocov <- '

  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  visual ~ x8 + x9

  x8 ~~ 0*x9
'

fitlav_regr <- lavaan(HS_model_regr, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE, auto.fix.first = TRUE, auto.var=TRUE)
fitlav_regr_cov <- lavaan(HS_model_regr_cov, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE, auto.fix.first = TRUE, auto.var=TRUE)
fitlav_regr_nocov <- lavaan(HS_model_regr_nocov, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE, auto.fix.first = TRUE, auto.var=TRUE)

The first interesting thing that I noticed is that where I might interpret Model 1 as having the covariance implicitly fixed to zero, lavaan interprets it as implicitly free.  That is, Model 1 and Model 2 are the same, and differ from Model 3.

lavInspect(fitlav_regr, what='free')$psi
lavInspect(fitlav_regr_cov, what='free')$psi
lavInspect(fitlav_regr_nocov, what='free')$psi

fitMeasures(fitlav_regr, fit.measures=c('chisq', 'df'))
fitMeasures(fitlav_regr_cov, fit.measures=c('chisq', 'df'))
fitMeasures(fitlav_regr_nocov, fit.measures=c('chisq', 'df'))

Only Model 1 with the implicit specification produces the unexpected independence model.  Both explicit specifications produce the expected independence model.

as.data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitlav_regr))
as.data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitlav_regr_cov))
as.data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitlav_regr_nocov))

I have not parsed the code in sufficient detail to understand why that happens.  However, it seems like good practice to avoid the implicit specification and, as you did, to always double check that you obtained the focal model and baseline model that you expected, especially when using convenience parameters.

Thanks again for bringing this phenomenon to my attention.  I generally avoid using the convenience parameters or the wrapper functions. So, I would not have encountered this phenomenon on my own.

Keith

messages.body_plain:
> The first interesting thing that I noticed is that where I might
> interpret Model 1 as having the covariance implicitly fixed to zero,
> lavaan interprets it as implicitly free.  That is, Model 1 and Model 2
> are the same, and differ from Model 3.

That is correct. But it is a side-effect of the auto.var = TRUE
argument, in combination with fixed.x = FALSE. If you want to be very
explicit, use this:

HS_model_regr <- '
visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
visual ~ x8 + x9

visual ~~ visual
textual ~~ textual

x1 ~~ x1
x2 ~~ x2
x3 ~~ x3
x4 ~~ x4
x5 ~~ x5
x6 ~~ x6

x8 ~~ x8
x9 ~~ x9

'

fit <- lavaan(HS_model_regr, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE,
auto.fix.first = TRUE)

Here, no covariance is added for x8 ~~ x9

So the tricky part is the auto.var = TRUE argument, which makes a
distinction between 'exogenous' and 'endogenous' (observed) variables.
In fact, this also works:

HS_model_regr <- '
visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
visual ~ x8 + x9

x8 ~~ x8
x9 ~~ x9

'

fit <- lavaan(HS_model_regr, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x=FALSE,

auto.fix.first = TRUE, auto.var = TRUE)

Here, the exogenous variances are already specified, so auto.var will
not intervene, and no further covariance(s) are added.

The logic behind all this is the following: under the default fixed.x =
TRUE, we certainly want to include the covariance. If we switch from
fixed.x = TRUE to fixed.x = FALSE, we just want to bring the exogenous
parameters (means, variances, covariance) to the model. And -by design-
this switch should not impose any further restrictions. That is why the
covariance is included (by default), if you rely on auto.var = TRUE to
include the (exogenous) variances.

As for the baseline model: if the exogenous covariances are unrestricted
in the user-specified h0 model, then they will also be unrestricted in
the baseline model.

Yves.

You can add a correlation between an error and a predictor by adding correlations to the model

# define analysis model
mModel <- '
F2 ~ F1
F3 ~ F1 + F2
F4 ~ F2 + F3

F4 ~~ F2

F4 ~ F2 + F3

Thanks Mikko. Actually, I've tried this before; adding F4 ~~ F2 and F4 ~~ F3 leads to an identification problem, and adding only F4 ~~ F2 to severely biased results for at least one of the regression coefficients.

One possible solution is to create an instrumental variable I4 as indicated below, and then use it in the regression equation for F4. The results are then identical to those of the 2SLS analysis that I conducted.

mModel <- '
# instrumental variable
I4 =~ F1
# path model

F2 ~ F1
F3 ~ F1 + F2

F4 ~ F2 + F3 + I4
'
In this specific case, this is equivalent to adding F1 as a predictor of F4. However, the link F1 -> F4 does not exist at the population, and thus I would get a false positive if I had added that link.

I just thought that there was a better way to do this with lavaan. The approach above would not work if the instrumental variable were more complex; e.g., aggregated two or more  instruments. In econometrics, instrumental variables are typically created as composites.

Ned

messages.body_plain:
Yves,
Thanks for explaining the rationale behind the auto.var behavior.  It is good to know that it is a feature and not a bug.  Here are a few thoughts on documenting the feature so that more users can put it to use.

lavOptions.html currently states "auto.var: If TRUE, the residual variances and the variances of exogenous latent variables are included in the model and set free."  Perhaps this could be expanded to add:  "When lavaan encounters model syntax with no explicit variances or covariances for exogenous variables and fixed.x = FALSE, lavaan attempts to emulate the fixed.x specification by adding these to the focal model and baseline model.  When the model syntax includes such parameters, this will not occur."

The advent of fixed.x modeling means that there is no longer a unitary convention about what the default baseline model.  Perhaps it would be helpful for lavaan to alert the user when the baseline model is not the full independence model: "Note: Your baseline model includes at least one free covariance."

At some point in the future, perhaps it would be helpful to add the baseline model parameter table to the objects returned by lavaan, and give this a what= value for lavInspect.

Keith

messages.subject_clean: A Question on simsem (This is a simsem bug)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

That looks like a bug in simsem. The workaround is to allow simsem to automatically add some parameters instead of specifying them manually.

analyzeModel <- "
f1 =~ y11 + y12 + y13 + y14 + y15 + y16 + y17 + y18
f2 =~ y21 + y22 + y23 + y24 + y25 + y26 + y27 + y28
"

If you want to see what the problem is, you can troubleshoot as follows. After the error message, do

Error in names(coef) <- lab :
  'names' attribute [35] must be the same length as the vector [33]

> traceback()
4: runRep(simConds[[i]], ...)
3: FUN(X[[i]], …)
..

>From this output, you can see that the line that caused the problem is "names(coef) <- lab” in function simsem:::runRep. Then you print out the function as a list

as.list(body(simsem:::runRep))

from which you can see that the line is included in the 50th step. Then you print that step

as.list(as.list(body(simsem:::runRep))[[50]])

and note that the line is in the 3rd step inside that step. Doing recursively, you end up with

as.list(as.list(as.list(as.list(as.list(as.list(as.list(as.list(body(simsem:::runRep))[[50]])[[3]])[[3]])[[3]])[[2]])[[4]])[[4]])

and note that the line is the 19th step in that.

Then you set up tracing:

trace(simsem:::runRep,browser, at = list(c(50,3,3,3,2,4,4,19)))

Running the code after that allows you to inspect what R is doing right before the error. At least the following commands are useful for understanding why the label and coefficient length do not match

print(coef)
print(lab)
summary(fit)

After you are done, you can remove tracing by doing

untrace(simsem:::runRep)

The  bug is that the coefficients includes only free parameters whereas the labels includes both free parameters and parameters that were constrained by user.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: endogeneity in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: endogeneity in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Ned,

While your explanation has some correct elements, it is not entirely correct: In 2sls, you do not include IVs in the regression. Instead, in the first stage you regress all your original explanatory variables on the instruments, and then you use these fitted values as replacements for the original explanatory variables in the second stage regression.

But this post finally clarified what is it that you want to do:

Your population model was

F2 ~ F1
F3 ~ F1 + F2

F4 ~ F1 + F2 + F3

And the estimated model was

F2 ~ F1
F3 ~ F1 + F2
F4 ~ F2 + F3

So yes, F2 and F3 are endogenous regressors in that model because they both correlated with the omitted variable F1. You are right that you can obtain consistent estimates if you include F1 as a predictor of F4, but that has nothing to do with instrumental variables or 2sls. If we have an omitted variable, then an ideal solution is of course to get data for that variable and then include it to the model. Instrumental variables address the scenario where that is not possible. To qualify as an instrument, a variable must meet the exclusion criterion, which means that it should not be correlated with the error term of the focal regression. In your model X1 faisl this criterion because it has a unique effect in the population and is therefore not a valid instrument.

Mikko

> On 15 Nov 2017, at 16.50, Ned Kock <ned...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Mikko: In a 2SLS analysis, in-model endogeneity is controlled for by the creation of instrumental variables (IVs) for certain endogenous variables, and the inclusion of the IVs in regression equations. The classic approach used in econometrics is to create IVs as composites that aggregate instruments. The instruments are exogenous variables that influence the endogenous variables in question only via indirect effects.

There are several conceptual similarities among Bollen's MIIV approach, Rosseel's Factor Score Path Analysis, and my own Factor-Based PLS-SEM method. The latter, explained in the report linked below, is the one I mentioned to you in Macau.

The key to estimating factors is, in my view, something akin to the variation sharing technique (see link below). Variants of the Factor-Based PLS-SEM methods have been implemented in WarpPLS (warppls.com <http://warppls.com>) for at least 3 years now.

http://cits.tamiu.edu/kock/pubs/journals/2017/Kock_Sexton_2017_IJSDS_PLSAcctMeasError.pdf

Ned

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I wanted to see if the sem of lavaan gives us unbiased estimators in a given simulation structure.

This is a part of my simulation code:

set.seed(123)
X = runif(sample_size,0,1)
M = 0.8*X + rnorm(sample_size)
M_star = as.numeric(M>=2)
Y = 3 + 0.5*M_star + 0.2*X + rnorm(sample_size,0,2)
Data = data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M_star = M_star)

model="Y ~ a*X + b*M_star
       M_star ~ c*X"

fit=sem(model,data=Data,ordered = "M_star")
parameterEstimates(fit)

My result was:

     lhs  op    rhs label    est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1      Y   ~      X     a -0.040 0.078 -0.510   0.61   -0.194    0.114
2      Y   ~ M_star     b  0.267 0.040  6.634   0.00    0.188    0.346
3 M_star   ~      X     c  0.754 0.074 10.172   0.00    0.608    0.899
4 M_star   |     t1        1.967 0.047 41.668   0.00    1.875    2.060
5      Y  ~~      Y        3.990 0.059 67.086   0.00    3.874    4.107
6 M_star  ~~ M_star        1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
7 M_star ~*~ M_star        1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
8      Y  ~1               3.013 0.041 73.990   0.00    2.933    3.093
9 M_star  ~1               0.000 0.000     NA     NA    0.000    0.000

Those two estimates of a and b (-0.04 and 0.267 respectively) in yellow were largely deviated from the true values (0.2 and 0.5). I am pretty sure that the estimate of b indicates something else than the coefficient of the regression of Y on M_star. Why can't my estimates come closer to the true parameters?

Thank you,
Yunsung

messages.body_plain:
> Unfortunately, I don't know how to examine if the rsquare for each item is significant. Can anyone please show me how to inspect the significant of rsquare for each item in my model?

It is not an estimated model parameter, so there is not a significance test for it.  You could calculate it as a user-defined variable using the := operator to get an estimated SE and CI using the delta method.  Or you could use the bootstrapLavaan() function to get a bootstrap CI for each r-squared.

messages.subject: Re: Continuous predictor, binary mediator and continuous outcome
messages.subject_clean: Continuous predictor, binary mediator and continuous outcome
messages.body_plain:
> I am pretty sure that the estimate of b indicates something else than the coefficient of the regression of Y on M_star. Why can't my estimates come closer to the true parameters?

You are correct.  M_Star is a dummy code, and your population value is the effect of the dummy code (i.e., a group-mean difference in Y, given X).  But because M_Star is endogenous in your model, lavaan does not estimate the effect of the dummy code, it estimates the effect of a latent item-response that is assumed to be normally distributed (do some reading on probit regression to see what is happening when you regress the dummy code M_Star on X).  Thus, the estimated effect is associated not with a 1-unit increase in M_Star (i.e., a group-mean difference in Y given X), but rather with a 1-unit increase in the latent item-response.  I don't know of a clear way to translate your population value of b into the corresponding population value that will be estimated by the model, but you can try asking on SEMNET.

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Model1 <- 'PVCX100 ~ logPDD_HA + HPD_A

fit1=sem(Model1,data = D1,na.rm=TRUE)

messages.subject_clean: Mediated moderation model with control variables
messages.body_plain:
> Is it correct that I didn't include an interaction then?

It is not correct or incorrect, but I do think it is somewhat more intuitive to test whether meditating/indirect effects are moderated by a grouping variable using a multigroup model instead of a single-group model with product terms.

> my outcome variable Y is 0/1)

Be aware that this is a probit regression when you are interpreting effects on Y.  Regardless of the correct interpretation, it does not affect the way you can compare effects across groups to test for moderation (of direct or indirect effects).

> model<-'# direct effect
> Y ~ c(c1,c2)*X + c(b1,b2)*M
> # mediator
> M ~ c(a1,a2)*X
> Y ~ c(b1,b2)*M

You included the effect of M on Y twice (the top and bottom lines above).  You should delete one of them to avoid confusion or later mistakes. Usually lavaan gives a warning about duplicate entries.

> #indirect effect
> ab1 := a1*b1
> ab2 := a2*b2
> #total effect
> tot1 := c1 + (a1*b1)
> tot2 := c2 + (a2*b2)'

Correct calculation of effects in both groups.  But in order to test moderation, you need to calculate differences between groups.

ab_diff := ab1 - ab2

The test of that difference is the test of moderated mediation (i.e., whether the indirect effect is moderated by Mod).

> fit <- sem(model, data = data, group = "Mod", test = "bootstrap")

You are only requesting a Bollen-Stine bootstrap for the model-fit test statistic, but not bootstrap SEs  (that would require the argument se = "boot").  But I'm not saying either are necessary.  If you have a large enough sample size for bootstrapping to work (i.e., that sampling error is minimal, so a random sample is a good representation of the population), then your sample size is also large enough not to need bootstrap SEs to test your indirect effects.  That is, at large N the indirect effects will have approximately normal sampling distributions, so the delta method lavaan uses to derive SEs would already yield approximately nominal Type I error rates.

> If I would want to include controls, do they also need moderator-specific parameters for them?

If you include covariate effects, then different slopes across groups implies that the covariate interacts with Mod.  In that case, the effect of X on M (which is a mean difference in M) is not comparable across groups (levels of Mod).  You can first test whether the slope(s) of the covariate(s) are equal across groups by giving them the same labels across groups to constrain them to equality, then comparing the fit of the models with and without equality constraints.  If you cannot reject the null hypothesis of equal covariate effects across groups, then you can compare the effect of X across groups in a subsequent test.

This is the "homogeneity of slopes assumption" for comparing "adjusted means" in ANCOVA, so you can search Google about that for a more detailed explanation.

> Do I need to consider something if I would want to use a categorical variable with 4 levels?

You would need to have a vector of 4 labels for parameters across 4 groups

Y ~ c(c1,c2,c3,c4)*X + c(b1,b2,b3,b4)*M

With only 2 groups, there is only 1 pairwise comparison, but with 4 groups, there are 6 pairwise comparisons.  So you should first test an omnibus null hypothesis of equality of the indirect effect across all groups, by constraining all component direct paths to equality

a1 == a2
a2 == a3
a3 == a4
b1 == b2
b2 == b3
b3 == b4

Then define your 6 difference parameters in the syntax of the less constrained model only if the omnibus null is rejected.

ab_12 := ab1 - ab2
ab_13 := ab1 - ab3
ab_14 := ab1 - ab4
ab_23 := ab2 - ab3
ab_24 := ab2 - ab4
ab_34 := ab3 - ab4

messages.body_plain:
> Panel size: T = 10 and number of firms = 355.

Does that mean 10 time points?  You only model a single instance of each variable below, so is this only using 1 timepoint?

> 1. Can you use above code to find mediation in panel data?

You can, if you label the parameters and define the indirect effect(s) you want to use to test mediation.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

> If yes, what happens to unobserved individual heterogeneity.

What do you mean?   Have you stacked all timepoints on top of each other in "long" format, so that each person has T = 10 rows of data?  If so, then this analysis is invalid because you are not accounting for observations being nested within individuals.  You could fit a multilevel SEM, which is very experimental at this point, or you could put the data in wide format (355 independent rows, so no issue with latent heterogeneity) and run a cross-lagged panel model.

> 2. Do I need to include the control variables in the regression model?

Depends on your theory and the background literature.  This isn't a software question.

> 2. If above method is correct, what should we conclude from the output? In case of HPD_A, there is no mediation. But in case of logPDD_HA, can we conclude a partial mediation?

Again, read the tutorial I linked to, showing you how to calculate indirect effects that you want to test.  Other than that, your other questions lead me to believe you should read a lot more about mediation models to inform how you specify them and draw inferences from them.  Other than textbooks and articles, SEMNET is a good resource for general SEM questions like that:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

As long as you have no predictors, this is indeed ok. What type = "ov"

matrix (and perhaps the intercepts) to project those latent variables to
the outcome variables. So yes, in this case, they do give you
'predicted' (or model-based) values for the repeated measures.

messages.body_plain:
Angeline--
     Yes, this is predictable. The indProd() function offers an option, match, which if FALSE multiplies all indicators by all indicators (as you chose, apparently), but if TRUE it mutiplies the first indicators of each set, the second indicators of each set, and so forth. Multiplying all by all creates a complex pattern of correlated residuals--because the same x1, for example, is now part of multiple different observed variables. It also multiplies (pardon me) the number of nonnormal observed variables in your model.
     You have choices. A recent paper by Foldnes and Hagtvedt (2014) recommends the all by all over the matching approach. You can use that approach, but to obtain a correctly specified model you must include the free residual covariances implied. If x1 is one of your original indicators, then all of the product indicator that used x1 as a component will now have residual covariance. You may have trouble getting such a model to converge.
     The other approach is to use Herbert Marsh's matching. That obviates the need for residual covariances but may be statistically inferior, at the margin.
http://psycnet.apa.org/journals/met/19/3/444/
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
> I guess I need to investigate parceling approaches to use Marsh's match approach as I have unequal numbers of indicators .

The matching procedure assumes an equal number of indicators per factor.  If you read the references provided on the ?indProd help page, you will find an example analysis with appropriate residual covariances in the residual-centering article.  Residual centering is better than mean-centering, but double-mean-centering has additional advantages you might want (again, the article is in the help-page references).

Terrence D. Jorgensen

I've been learning SEM and attempted to replicate the findings of a mediation analysis in a published paper. The coefficients I get with SEM match the paper very closely. However, the fit statistics are confusing and I'm having trouble tracking down information on how to diagnose what is going on.

The chi-square statistic is 42.3 with 5 degrees of freedom indicating that my data are extremely rare if the null hypothesis (all covariances are zero) is in fact true. But the first one is a Zero and I don't know what the test is.

messages.subject_clean: How to diagnose "strange" fit statistics like RMSEA = 0?
messages.body_plain:
Regression models like this one are typically saturated, meaning that the target model has 0 degrees of freedom, and its "fit" is perfect by default. That mean chi-square = 0, CFI = 1, RMSEA = 0, SRMR = 0. None of these results offer any comment on the quality of your model--they are all the immediate result of the model being saturated.

messages.subject: Resources for DWLS in ordinal sem
messages.subject_clean: Resources for DWLS in ordinal sem
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am researching the inner resources of adolescents, using sem to determine directionality. I have ordinal measures and have decided not to use them as continuous variables for a number of reasons. The data are survey data and have some attrition. I have weighting variables but due to the data being ordinal, I cannot use Lavaan survey.

I’ve read all the lavaan paperwork for ordinal sem but I was wondering if there were any other resources that people can suggest in regards to decisions such as using pairwise versus listwise deletion where data may not be MCAR, so that I can note this in my thesis?

My models are pretty strong in regards to fit. I do have the warning regarding empty cells, but I am not concerned about this as all of my variables have five categories and I have the paper that indicates that Lavaan deals with this okay.

messages.subject: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.subject_clean: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have two different models, one being a model with direct effects, one being a model with mediation effects. I would like to compare these two to see which one better fits the data. Hence, I used the anova() function. However, anova (model1, model2) gives me a different result than anova(model2, model1).
Would you have an idea why this is happening? How then interpret my results?
I am just starting with SEM and Lavaan so perhaps is there a simple explanation?

Below are the two models and the associated anova results:

MODELS
------------

model1 <-'
#measurement model
PD =~ PD1 + PD2 + PD3
PR=~ PR1 + PR2 + PR3
PO =~ PO1 + PO2 + PO3
NS =~ NS1 + NS2 + NS3
JSS =~ JSS1 + JSS2 + JSS3

#Direct effect
JSS ~ d1*PO + d2*PD + d3*PR + d4*NS
'
model1.fit <- sem(model1, data=myframe.df)

model2 <-'
#measurement model
PD =~ PD1 + PD2 + PD3
PR=~ PR1 + PR2 + PR3
PO =~ PO1 + PO2 + PO3
NS =~ NS1 + NS2 + NS3
JSS =~ JSS1 + JSS2 + JSS3

#Direct effect
JSS ~ d1*PO + d2*PD + d3*PR

#Mediator effect
NS ~ ns1*PO
NS ~ ns2*PD
NS ~ ns3*PR
JSS ~ ns*NS

#Indirect effect
ns1ns:=ns1*ns
ns2ns:=ns2*ns
ns3ns:=ns3*ns

#total effect
total1:= d1 + (ns1*ns)
total2:= d2 + (ns2*ns)
total3:= d3 + (ns3*ns)
'
model2.fit <- sem(model2, data=myframe.df)

print(anova(model2.fit, model2.fit))

RESULTS:
--------------

Chi Square Difference Test

             Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651
model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651  6.126e-10       0  < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
Chi Square Difference Test

             Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651
model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651 -6.126e-10       0          1

So... in one case the anova/chi sqr tells me that the mediation effects add value to the model and that the most complicated model (partial mediation, model 2) should be retained as fitting best the data (chi sqr is significant) while the second anova tells me the opposite...

Any help would be much appreciated!

Many thanks,

Nicolas

messages.subject: Re: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.subject_clean: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.body_plain:
> Chi Square Difference Test
>
>               Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
> model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651
> model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651  6.126e-10       0  < 2.2e-16 ***

Note that the 'Df diff' (the difference between the degrees of freedom
of the two models) is zero. So the models have the same number of
parameters. Therefore, they can not be compared with a classic
chi-square difference test.

The 'correct' answer here would be p.value = NA (which is what you will
get in lavaan dev 0.6-1).

>               Df    AIC    BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
> model2JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651
> model1JS.fit 80 5400.2 5523.5 97.651 -6.126e-10       0          1

So, usually, anova() will automatically reorder the models according to
their degrees of freedom, but not here. Therefore you end of with a tiny
tiny negative number -6.126e-10. And it so happens that

 > (1 - pchisq(-1, df = 0))
[1] 1

It should be NA again. Compare this to

 > pchisq(-1, df = 0, lower.tail = TRUE)
[1] 0

and it becomes clear that the p-value is not defined if df = 0.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.body_plain:
Nicholas,
Actually, reproducing analyses from a book sounds like a very good strategy.  However, it is hard to believe that a SEM book would give an example of attempting a chi-square difference test for non-nested models with the same df.  Perhaps something got lost in translation from the original to your code.

Ed knows the history of this better than I do, but one strategy for comparing non-nested models is the following.
(1) Construct a meta-model that includes the parameters from both models of interest.
(2) Conduct a chi-square difference test comparing each model to the meta-model.
(3) If the results differ, favor the model that does not differ in fit from the meta-model.
So, if you really do have a reason to compare such models, this offers one option.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: Optimize bootstrapping in parallel
messages.subject_clean: Optimize bootstrapping in parallel
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Three suggestions:

1) If you are running a Monte Carlo simulation that does bootstrap in each Monte Carlo replication, then it is easier to parallelize on the Monte Carlo level than the bootstrap level

2) Throwing more hardware to the problem is an easy way to significantly speed up things. If your university has a computer cluster, you might be able to run the simulation with 2400 instead of 24 cores.

3) Instead of using boot on one of the main lavaan functions (sem, cfa), prepare the starting values and parse the model before bootstrapping and then apply bootstrap to private functions that do the actual estimation. You can use profiling http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Profiling.html to see where the code spends time and if you can move some of that to preprocessing.

4) decrease the number of iterations to exit problematic estimations more quickly.

What exactly is the best way depends on what specifically you want to do with bootstrap.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.subject_clean: Model comparison = anova results inconsistency?
messages.body_plain:
Nicolas,
   Remember that SEM is a form of analysis of covariance structure (or more generally moment structure).  You are modeling the covariance matrix, not the dependent variables.  As a result, certain concepts from generalized linear models, like the null model with just an intercept, do not carry over directly.  In SEM, the term 'null model' might instead refer to a model in which all the variables are uncorrelated.  (Moreover, by default, all variables are assumed centered in SEM, which results in zero intercepts.)  Likewise, residuals in SEM are covariance residuals, not the difference between predicted and observed values of the dependent variables.

  There are some other differences in style but not in substance between your two model syntax objects.  However, yes, the zeros are the substantive differences that fix the three effect coefficients to zero and change the df by 3.

  You can accomplish the same thing simply by omitting the corresponding variable from the right-hand-side of the line of model syntax, or omitting the entire line if you are not retaining anything on the right-hand-side.  For example, commenting out the lines would have the same effect as your fixed zeros.

# NS ~ ns1*PO
# NS ~ ns2*PD
# NS ~ ns3*PR

  You can (and this is generally a good idea) check lavaan's interpretation of your model syntax by viewing either the parameter table or the matrix representations of your model.

lavaanify(model1)
lavInspect(model1.fit, what='free')

  Just a word of caution.  Bentler & Bonett (1980) made a useful distinction between parameter nesting and covariance nesting.  If the parameters in one model form a subset of the parameters in another, as in your example, then the models are parameter nested.  Parameter nesting is sufficient but not necessary for covariance nesting.  The most famous example is that a one-factor model is covariance nested, but not parameter nested, within a model with freely estimated covariances for all pairs of variables.

Keith

Bentler, P. M., & Bonett, D. G. (1980). Significance tests and goodness-of-fit in the analysis of covariance structures. Psychological Bulletin, 88, 588-606.

------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

I know that "lavaan" function allows a full control and does not automatically create residual variables (unless you explicitly tell it so) but how to write a model with error latent variables is not clear to me.

Hi,

When you say that you get an error message, it is always a good idea to tell the list what the message was. If I understood it correctly, this problem relates to how the model is represented as matrices. The following code example shows how it does not work and then shows a workaround.

Mikko

library(lavaan)

# This does not work

model <- '
  # measurement model
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
# regressions
dem60 ~ ind60
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
# error correlation
y1 ~~ dem65'

fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(fit, standardized=TRUE)

# This does work

model <- '
  # measurement model
ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
LATENTy1 =~ y1
dem60 =~ LATENTy1 + y2 + y3 + y4
dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
# regressions
dem60 ~ ind60
dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
# error correlation
LATENTy1 ~~ dem65'

fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(fit, standardized=TRUE)

# See https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38560145/how-to-specify-correlation-between-latent-and-observed-variable-in-lavaan

messages.body_plain:
This is due to the LISREL representation that is used by lavaan. In
LISREL, there is no such a thing as a covariance between an observed and
a latent variable. The only way out (for now) is to create a
single-indicator latent variable, as Mikko pointed out. One day, lavaan
may do this automatically (as it is already doing if you are using a
regression instead).

Amos is using the RAM representation, where these covariances are just
part of the 'symmetric' matrix.

Yves.
