Hi again,

Thank you for your prompt answer.
I know that bootstrapping has nothing to do with the warning message, but actually, the bootstrapping is the aim as to why we intend to re-apply the model in R Lavaan. When I ran the bootstrapping of the model using only 100 samples in AMOS, the program hanged and kept working for a long time (54 hours) before I ended it. So, the bootstrapping is what we concern about right now. I need to report the CIs of some direct, indirect, and total effects in the model. Thus, I really appreciate your help in this.

Regarding of whether I fixed the variance of any error to zero, I really didn't do so explicitly using the model syntax "0*variable", but I am not aware if the "sem" function did it automatically or not. Below you can find my complete syntax model and the sem function. The parts in bold font are those I updated upon your suggestion.

# create a model
model <- '# latent variable definitions
            Entity_Ability           =~ mind_a_g_16_Invrt + mind_a_g_12_Invrt + mind_a_f_15
            Mastery_Goal          =~ goal_M_02 + goal_M_05 + goal_M_03
            Innov                       =~ Innov_E_02 + Innov_E_09 + Innov_L_13_Invrt
            Hierarchy                 =~ oca_HIE_24 + oca_HIE_20 + oca_HIE_16
            e52                         =~ growth_REW_06
            Sprt_Rwd_Mang     =~ e52 + growth_ENC_01 + growth_ENC_02
            Oper_Capa_team      =~ growth_COS_16 + growth_TES_17 + growth_TES_18
            Avoidance                =~ goal_A_13 + goal_A_12 + goal_A_11

            # regressions
            Sprt_Rwd_Mang      ~ HR_SRM*Hierarchy
            Mastery_Goal         ~ ENTT_MG*Entity_Ability + SRM_MG*Sprt_Rwd_Mang
            Oper_Capa_team    ~ SRM_OCT*Sprt_Rwd_Mang
            Avoidance              ~ HR_AVOD*Hierarchy
            Innov                      ~ MG_INNOV*Mastery_Goal + SRM_INNOV*Sprt_Rwd_Mang + OCT_INNOV*Oper_Capa_team + AVOD_INNOV*Avoidance

            # residual (co)variances
            e52                         ~~ Oper_Capa_team
            growth_REW_06     ~~ growth_ENC_01 + oca_HIE_16
            goal_A_12               ~~ mind_a_g_12_Invrt

            # indirect effects
            indEff_ENTT                := ENTT_MG*MG_INNOV
            indEff_HR_AVD           := HR_AVOD*AVOD_INNOV
            indEff_HR_SRM_dir     := HR_SRM*SRM_INNOV
            indEff_HR_SRM_MG   := HR_SRM*SRM_MG*MG_INNOV
            indEff_HR_SRM_OCT  := HR_SRM*SRM_OCT*OCT_INNOV
            indEff_SRM_MG          := SRM_MG*MG_INNOV
            indEff_SRM_OCT         := SRM_OCT*OCT_INNOV

            # total effect
            total_SRM                  := SRM_INNOV + indEff_SRM_MG + indEff_SRM_OCT

Le mercredi 29 novembre 2017 04:25:07 UTC, kma...@aol.com a écrit :
> Nicolas,
>    Remember that SEM is a form of analysis of covariance structure (or more generally moment structure).  You are modeling the covariance matrix, not the dependent variables.  As a result, certain concepts from generalized linear models, like the null model with just an intercept, do not carry over directly.  In SEM, the term 'null model' might instead refer to a model in which all the variables are uncorrelated.  (Moreover, by default, all variables are assumed centered in SEM, which results in zero intercepts.)  Likewise, residuals in SEM are covariance residuals, not the difference between predicted and observed values of the dependent variables.
>
>   There are some other differences in style but not in substance between your two model syntax objects.  However, yes, the zeros are the substantive differences that fix the three effect coefficients to zero and change the df by 3.
>
>   You can accomplish the same thing simply by omitting the corresponding variable from the right-hand-side of the line of model syntax, or omitting the entire line if you are not retaining anything on the right-hand-side.  For example, commenting out the lines would have the same effect as your fixed zeros.
>
> # NS ~ ns1*PO
> # NS ~ ns2*PD
> # NS ~ ns3*PR
>
>   You can (and this is generally a good idea) check lavaan's interpretation of your model syntax by viewing either the parameter table or the matrix representations of your model.
>
> lavaanify(model1)
> lavInspect(model1.fit, what='free')
>
>   Just a word of caution.  Bentler & Bonett (1980) made a useful distinction between parameter nesting and covariance nesting.  If the parameters in one model form a subset of the parameters in another, as in your example, then the models are parameter nested.  Parameter nesting is sufficient but not necessary for covariance nesting.  The most famous example is that a one-factor model is covariance nested, but not parameter nested, within a model with freely estimated covariances for all pairs of variables.
>
> Keith
>
> Bentler, P. M., & Bonett, D. G. (1980). Significance tests and goodness-of-fit in the analysis of covariance structures. Psychological Bulletin, 88, 588-606.
>
> ------------------------
> Keith A. Markus
> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
> Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
> http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
>

Dear Mikko.

Thanks for the suggestions. A few questions:

1. Why would that be faster? I think I tried that and it seemed slower.... Maybe I did it wrong?

3. Can you explain a bit more how is it done? If you have an example code for it that would be great.

4. I can decrease the number of iteration. It's 1000 right now. I'm afraid any less than that going to be not enough for stable CIs. What do you mean by 'exit problematic estimations more quickly'?

Thanks!!!

Sent from my iPhone

On 28 Nov 2017, at 21:25, Mikko Rönkkö <mikko....@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi,

Three suggestions:

1) If you are running a Monte Carlo simulation that does bootstrap in each Monte Carlo replication, then it is easier to parallelize on the Monte Carlo level than the bootstrap level

2) Throwing more hardware to the problem is an easy way to significantly speed up things. If your university has a computer cluster, you might be able to run the simulation with 2400 instead of 24 cores.

3) Instead of using boot on one of the main lavaan functions (sem, cfa), prepare the starting values and parse the model before bootstrapping and then apply bootstrap to private functions that do the actual estimation. You can use profiling http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Profiling.html to see where the code spends time and if you can move some of that to preprocessing.

4) decrease the number of iterations to exit problematic estimations more quickly.

What exactly is the best way depends on what specifically you want to do with bootstrap.

Mikko

Hi All,

Apologies if this has already been discussed before.

I have two students who are attempting to replicate results using a correlation table in Lavaan. When they use the correlation table as an object, they are both able to replicate the results that were previously published. When they use the getcov function + the cor2cov to transform their data from a correlation matrix to a covariance matrix, both of their results appear to become much poorer model fits. It also appears that when using "inspect(modelname, what = "sampstat")" in their model, that a covariance matrix is created, but this matrix is different than one created manually by the students. Not sure what Lavaan is pulling on the back end.

My question: does Lavaan know that a correlation matrix needs to become a covariance matrix and creates one automatically? Or, does it treat it as a covariance matrix without any transformation?

I've attached code for both projects as well. Hopefully they are helpful

Thanks in advance,
-Jeff

messages.subject: Re: How to connect the residual (error) of latent variable to residual (error) of the observed variable
messages.subject_clean: How to connect the residual (error) of latent variable to residual (error) of the observed variable
messages.body_plain:
Alaa,
There are two ways to go about this. Mikko showed you one but your code suggests that you find the other more natural to think about.  The first way is to use the same approach that LISREL uses for path analysis and shadow an observed variable with a latent equivalent.  Mikko adapted that approach to your error covariance.

The second way is to delete the unique variance from the model and replace it with a latent variable.  In some ways, you may find this approach more intuitive because it avoids duplicate representations of the same variable.  In the following script y1UNIQE stands in for the unique variance of y1.  The variance of y1UNIQUE thus estimates the unique variance.  y1UNIQUE is represented the same way as other latent variables.  So, covariances are allowed in the phi matrix.

model2 <- '

  # measurement model
    ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

    y1UNIQUE =~ 0 # latent variable to take place of y1 uniqueness

    dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
    dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

    y1 ~~ 0*y1 # remove y1 unique variance
    y1UNIQUE ~~ y1UNIQUE # replacement y1 unique variance
  # regressions
    y1 ~ 1*y1UNIQUE # Fix effect coefficient for unique variance to 1

    dem60 ~ ind60
    dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
  # error correlation

    y1UNIQUE ~~ dem65'

fit2 <- sem(model2, data=PoliticalDemocracy)
summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE)

Just to clarify what Mikko said:  A single indicator can have a unique variance, but it is not usually possible to freely estimate that variance.  One typically has to fix it at a specified value prior to estimation.  That value need not be zero.  The approach given above avoids single indicators in your model syntax.  However, lavaan will include a fixed zero loading of y1UNIQUE on itself in its representation of the model.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

I'm testing a model that uses ratio constraints on the factor loadings of a single LV measured over time. My example should make this more clear.

model.ratio <-

'#measurement model

G1 =~ a1*T1I1 + a2*T1I2 + a3*T1I3 + a4*T1I4 + a5*T1I5

G2 =~ b1*T2I1 + b2*T2I2 + b3*T2I3 + b4*T2I4 + b5*T2I5

#ratio constraints
c == a1 / b1
c == a2 / b2
c == a3 / b3
c == a4 / b4
c == a5 / b5'

Lavaan rejects this because of my introduction of the ratio term "c" which is unspecified in the measurement model. An alternative here is manual entry of a ratio of a given size (e.g., .80) but I would rather have lavaan estimate the optimal ratio. Is there a work around to this issue?

Thanks. everyone
